The study titled Competence in the aquatic environment by students in the second cycle of early childhood education was published in the Sport TK Euro-American Journal of Sports Sciences in 2018, volume 7, issue 2, pages 73–79. It discusses the development of aquatic skills in young children. 2. Moderate risk of bias was identified due to confounding factors, as assessed by the ROBINS-I tool. 3. There was a moderate risk of bias in the measurement of outcomes, also evaluated using the ROBINS-I tool. 4. The study had a limited sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. 5. The 95% confidence interval and p-value could not be estimated using RevMan because the standard deviation of the intervention group was zero. 6. Similarly, the 95% confidence interval and p-value could not be calculated for the control group due to a standard deviation of zero. 7. There was significant variability in the results, which may impact the reliability of the conclusions. 8. Another study, Deep and shallow water effects on developing preschoolers’ aquatic skills, was published in the Journal of Human Kinetics in 2012, volume 32, pages 211–219. It examined the influence of water depth on preschoolers' ability to develop aquatic skills. 9. Moderate risk of bias was noted due to confounding factors, as per the ROBINS-I tool. 10. There was a moderate risk of bias in the classification of interventions, potentially due to recall bias, as assessed by the ROBINS-I tool. 11. A moderate risk of bias was also identified due to missing data, as per the ROBINS-I tool. 12. The study had a limited sample size, which may limit the robustness of the findings. 13. The authors reported only a 90% confidence interval, which does not align with the standard 95% confidence interval typically used in research. 14. Lack of blinding of participants and outcome assessors was noted, but this was deemed unlikely to affect the outcomes significantly. Other limitations were also present, as assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. 15. Partial η² was used as a measure of effect size, representing the proportion of total variability in each outcome attributable to the intervention. 16. Serious risk of bias due to confounding factors was identified in some studies, as per the ROBINS-I tool. 17. Serious risk of bias in the measurement of outcomes was also noted, as assessed by the ROBINS-I tool. 18. Large variability in results was observed, which may affect the reliability of the conclusions. 19. Lack of blinding of participants and outcome assessors was noted in some studies, as assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. 20. Limited sample size was a recurring issue across multiple studies, potentially affecting the generalizability of the findings. 21. Lack of randomization and allocation concealment was unclear in some studies, as assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. 22. Incomplete accounting of outcome events was noted in some studies, but reasons were provided, and there was no differential dropout between comparison groups. 23. Other limitations were present in several studies, as assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. 24. Some studies lacked data on the number of students per age group, which limits the ability to analyze age-specific outcomes. 25. The 95% confidence interval could not be calculated in some cases due to missing standard deviations. 26. Data in some studies represented the number of entries rather than the number of participants, which may affect the interpretation of results. 27. Water safety training, both in-water and out-of-water, was often part of broader educational programs. Studies compared the effectiveness of these programs to no training or alternative approaches. 28. One randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared educational programs with both water safety and basic swim skills training of differing lengths. 29. Observational studies reported that educational injury prevention programs may increase the ability to identify risks, such as toddler fall in water, and encourage safer behaviors, such as deciding to stop playing near water. 30. The effectiveness of water safety training as part of broader educational programs was evaluated in several studies, with varying levels of certainty in the evidence. 31. Some studies reported water safety knowledge outcomes separately for different grades, such as grades 1, 2, and 3. 32. The variability in results and lack of standardization in reporting outcomes were common limitations across studies. 33. The lack of randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessors were frequently noted as methodological limitations. 34. The studies highlighted the importance of combining water safety training with basic swim skills training to improve knowledge and behaviors related to water safety.
